turns.doctor_question: Hello, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, doctor. Thank you. Well, honestly, I'm just at my wit's end, which is why I made the appointment. I work down at the dry cleaners—I do laundry and dry cleaning work—and usually, you know, you have a system for these things. But I just... I cannot seem to keep my work in order anymore. 

It's like my brain just completely stalls out when I look at my station. I've got the claim tickets, you know, the little numbered ones, and then the register receipts, and on top of that, there are all these workshop notes for when someone needs a hem fixed or a tough stain treated, and then the actual customer jobs themselves... and it all just gets piled together. I try to make separate piles, I really do, but then someone comes in, or the bell on the door rings, and suddenly it's just one massive mountain of paper and clothes. 

I end up just standing there staring at it because I absolutely do not know what to handle first. It's embarrassing, really. At my age you'd think I'd have a handle on organizing a front counter, but I'll pick up a ticket, put it down, pick up a receipt, and I just... I'm completely drowning in the piles, and it's making my days just miserable because I can't figure out where to start.

symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient explicitly describes severe difficulty keeping their work in order, managing piles of tickets and receipts, and figuring out what tasks to handle first.

turns.doctor_question: Did these kinds of organization and attention problems start when you were a child?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, absolutely. Yes, it goes way, way back. I remember being in grade school, maybe third or fourth grade—Mrs. Gable's class, actually, I still remember her, she was a very strict woman—and she was always having to pull my mother aside at parent-teacher conferences. In fact, it wasn't just her, it was pretty much every teacher I had. 

They would always tell my mom the exact same thing. They'd say, "She's such a bright girl, she really is, but she is just completely scattered." And they weren't wrong! I was constantly talking out of turn. I just couldn't hold my thoughts in, you know? If a thought popped into my head, I just blurted it right out in the middle of a lesson without even raising my hand. 

And the papers... oh my goodness, my desk was like a black hole. I was always losing my homework papers, or permission slips, or just anything they handed out. They'd give me a worksheet and five minutes later it was crumpled at the bottom of my bag or just gone entirely. My teachers were constantly having to stand over my shoulder and give me reminders to actually finish my work, because I'd do the first two problems and then start drawing on the edges of the paper or staring at the ceiling or talking to the kid next to me. My poor mother, she tried so hard to get me organized back then with little colored folders and checklists, but it never stuck. It's just always been this way, even when I was little.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes being unable to sustain attention on schoolwork, doing only the first two problems before stopping.
symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient states she needed constant reminders from teachers to actually finish her work.
symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient mentions her mother tried hard to get her organized with folders and checklists, but it never stuck.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient reports her desk was a 'black hole' and she was always losing homework papers and permission slips.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes being easily distracted from work by staring at the ceiling or talking to the kid next to her.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient admits she couldn't hold her thoughts in and blurted them out in the middle of lessons without raising her hand.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever had a period of several days or more when you felt unusually energized or on edge, with a lot less need for sleep than usual?
turns.patient_response:
No, I can't say I have. I mean, my mind is always going a mile a minute, like I said, just spinning and spinning with all the things I'm supposed to be doing and all the things I'm forgetting to do. But it's not like... it's not a burst of energy, you know? It's more of an exhausting kind of busy in my head. 

And sleep... well, sleep is its own whole ordeal. I've always needed my sleep. If anything, I probably need more sleep than most people just because my brain tires me out so much during the day. I'll get into bed and my mind will still be racing about the dry cleaning tickets or whether I left the iron on at work—which I never do, but I always worry I did—but I'm physically just drained. I certainly don't have days where I feel like I could just skip sleeping and keep going. 

I actually had a friend, Brenda, who used to get like that. She'd stay up for three days straight rearranging her entire house, painting the living room at 2:00 AM, and she'd say she felt fantastic, like she could conquer the world. But me? Oh no. If I don't get my solid seven or eight hours, I am just a complete zombie the next day at the counter. Even more scattered than usual, if you can believe that. So no, I've never had anything like what Brenda had, just my regular, everyday messiness and feeling tired from trying to keep up with it all.

symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient mentions her mind spinning with 'all the things I'm forgetting to do,' indicating forgetfulness in daily activities.
symptom_reasoning.S038: The patient explicitly states her mind is 'always going a mile a minute,' 'spinning and spinning,' and 'racing' when she gets into bed.
symptom_reasoning.S056: The patient describes worrying about daily tasks like dry cleaning tickets and constantly worrying she left the iron on at work.
symptom_reasoning.S033: The patient denies the doctor's question about periods of feeling unusually energized or on edge, and contrasts herself with a friend who felt she could 'conquer the world.'
symptom_reasoning.S034: The patient explicitly states she does not experience a 'burst of energy' and denies having periods of high activity like her friend who painted at 2 AM.
symptom_reasoning.S036: The patient strongly denies a decreased need for sleep, stating she has always needed her sleep and cannot skip it without becoming a 'zombie.'

turns.doctor_question: How much are these attention and organization problems affecting your work or daily life right now?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, it's... it's affecting just about everything, honestly. It's really taking a toll. I mean, at the shop, it's gotten to the point where it's causing real, tangible issues. Like just last week, Mrs. Higgins came in for her husband's navy suit—he had a big lodge dinner or something important to go to—and I couldn't find it because I'd completely mixed up the tickets. The order ended up being late, and she was so upset, which I completely understand, but it was just awful. 

And the billing! Oh, the billing is an absolute nightmare lately. I'll be ringing someone up, and then I get distracted by, say, a really tough grease stain on a blouse hanging behind the counter, and I forget to actually process the payment right, or I hand them the wrong change, or I put the receipt in the wrong pile. It gets so confused. My boss has been getting so short with me, and there have been these really tense moments with the other staff because they end up having to cover for my mistakes or smooth things over when the customers get snippy. I don't blame them for being irritated, I really don't, but it just hurts my heart because I am trying so, so hard to keep it all straight.

And it's not just at the dry cleaners, it's bleeding into my personal life, too. I've always been very involved at my church—I go to First Baptist, over on Elm Street—and I usually help lead the planning committee for the spring bazaar and the Sunday potlucks. I love doing it, I've done it for years, but lately... well, I've actually had to step back from leading any of the planning. I had to tell them I couldn't do it this season. I'd show up to the meetings without the volunteer signup sheets, or I'd promise to call the rental place for the extra folding tables and then completely forget until the day before the event. 

I could just see the looks on the other ladies' faces. You know that tight-lipped smile people give you when they're really losing their patience? People were just getting so frustrated with me, and I felt terrible about it. So I just told them I needed a break this year, but really, the truth is I just can't keep all the moving parts straight in my head anymore. It's just too much. I hate feeling like I'm letting everyone down, everywhere I go. I mean, you try to keep a smile on, but when you're messing up at the job you've known for years and then you can't even organize a church event without people getting annoyed with you... it's just exhausting.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient describes making careless mistakes at work, such as mixing up tickets, handing out the wrong change, and putting receipts in the wrong pile.
symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient explicitly states they can no longer organize church events and struggle to keep all the moving parts straight in their head.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient mentions misplacing a customer's suit and showing up to meetings without necessary items like volunteer signup sheets.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient notes being easily distracted by extraneous stimuli, such as a grease stain on a blouse while trying to process a payment.
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient describes forgetting daily tasks, such as completely forgetting to call a rental place for tables until the day before an event.

turns.doctor_question: Do you spend a lot of time worrying about different things, even when there isn’t a clear reason to worry?
turns.patient_response:
Well, no, not exactly. I mean, I wouldn't call it worrying, not in the way you're talking about, like, sitting around fretting about the end of the world or getting sick or something like that. I don't really do that. 

It's more that my brain is just so full of all the things I'm supposed to be doing, like I said before. It's like a running checklist that never ends, and I'm always terrified I've missed something on it. So I'll be thinking, "Did I tag Mrs. Higgins' coat? Did I put the right change in the till? Did I call the church about the tables?" And that feels stressful, of course it does, because I'm always dropping the ball lately! But it's not a general worry about... I don't know, things out of the blue. It's very specific to the fact that I just can't seem to keep my ducks in a row. 

Like my sister, Diane, now she's a worrier. She'll call me up and she's worried about the weather, or if her son's car is making a funny noise, or if she left the stove on—which, to be fair, I worry about too, but only because I actually *do* forget things like that! But Diane, she just worries to worry, even when everything is perfectly fine. I don't have time for that kind of worrying, honestly. I'm too busy trying to figure out where I put my keys or if I actually processed that credit card payment at work. So, no, I don't think I worry just to worry. It's more of a panic about what I've forgotten this time.

symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient explicitly states they 'can't seem to keep my ducks in a row,' indicating difficulty organizing tasks.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient mentions being busy trying to figure out where they put their keys, indicating they often lose items.
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient describes frequently forgetting things in daily activities, such as whether they processed a payment, called the church, or left the stove on.
symptom_reasoning.S056: The patient explicitly denies worrying without a clear reason, stating they don't 'worry just to worry' like their sister does.
